newsitem.title: UK: UK ad industry finds Labour govt sympathetic.
newsitem.headline: UK ad industry finds Labour govt sympathetic.

text.p: Britain's top advertising trade organisation on Tuesday said the country's Labour government is proving sympathetic to the industry, although there are concerns related to a proposal to create a food standards agency.

The Labour government, elected last May 1 in a landslide victory over the Conversatives, is "...by and large is quite sympathetic to the industry," Lionel Stanbrook, deputy director general of the Advertising Association, told Reuters in a phone interview.

Prior to the election, which Labour had been widely tipped to win, there had been concerns that Labour might seek to introduce statutory regulation of at least some aspects of Britain's advertising industry to replace the existing self-regulatory system.

Stanbrook noted that concerns about Labour's attitude to the advertising industry had dissipated even in advance of the election. "It's been some time since I started relaxing about what Labour will do to advertising," he said. "It won't do anything -- it might even improve it."

Although Labour and Prime Minister Tony Blair may continue to cast a closer eye at the self-regulatory system than the Conservatives had, Stanbrook said the party has been proving itself to be friendly to business.
The Advertising Association, a federation of 27 trade and professional bodies, is now setting its sights on the Labour Party's annual conference, to be held in Brighton September 29 to October 3.
"The true story of our work at the Labour Party Conference is assuring people that the self-regulatory system does work," Stanbrook said.
"We are a little worried about the direction from the food standards agency," he added. A proposal for a food safety agency to oversee food safety was put forth shortly after the general election.
The proposal, however, remains in the early stages, and Stanbrook said the industry is confident there would be room to discuss any proposals related to advertising.

But while the proposed food safety agency is a top concern, Stanbrook said the Advertising Association will not devote many resources at the Labour Party Conference to the government's proposed tobacco advertising ban.
"We are not going to be making a song and dance about tobacco advertising," he said. "We will limit our response to restating our position that it is not about smoking but about advertising."
The Advertising Association has repeatedly said it opposes a tobacco ad ban because tobacco companies should enjoy the same freedom to advertise as any other industry selling a legal product.
Meanwhile, as the Advertising Association makes plans for the Labour Party Conference, the industry remains very quiet over the Tory Party Conference.
"We are not even going to the Tory Party conference," said one advertising industry source.
